metadata.summary: Diagnose HE clinically, reverse its triggers and protect the airway. Titrate lactulose safely and distinguish rifaximin guidance from its labeled recurrence indication.
metadata.application: Assess cognition, airway, glucose and triggers; select a safe route, prevent excess diarrhea and plan recurrence prevention with the caregiver.
keyPoints: Grade HE with the examination, not ammonia.
Target 2 to 3 soft stools without dehydration.
Separate acute rifaximin guidance from labeled recurrence prevention.

bodies.heading: Diagnose clinically
bodies.body: Hepatic encephalopathy is brain dysfunction related to liver impairment or portosystemic shunting. Reduced clearance and shunting allow gut-derived substances, including ammonia, to contribute to cognitive and motor changes. In cirrhosis, the diagnosis requires clinical assessment and exclusion of competing causes. Obtain baseline cognition and the time course from the patient and caregiver; assess attention, orientation, behavior, sleep, consciousness and asterixis. Asterixis alone is not enough to diagnose overt HE and also occurs in other metabolic disorders.

bodies.heading: Grade severity and protect the airway
bodies.body: Covert HE includes minimal HE detected with appropriate cognitive testing and West Haven grade 1. Overt HE is grade 2 or higher: temporal disorientation and lethargy in grade 2, marked confusion and somnolence in grade 3, and coma in grade 4. Grade the clinical examination rather than an ammonia concentration; Glasgow Coma Scale can supplement high-grade assessment. Severe impaired consciousness or aspiration risk requires urgent monitored care and airway assessment. Do not give an unprotected, obtunded patient oral medication simply because lactulose is indicated.

bodies.heading: Find precipitants and dangerous mimics
bodies.body: Check glucose promptly and assess infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, constipation, dehydration or excessive diuresis, kidney dysfunction, electrolyte abnormalities and sedating drugs. Review opioids, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, sleep medicines, alcohol and other exposures. Infection, metabolic encephalopathy and HE can coexist. Evaluate new focal deficits, seizures or head trauma urgently for neurological disease; routine brain imaging is not needed for every typical recurrent HE episode without concerning findings. In a hospitalized patient with ascites and suspected infection, diagnostic paracentesis helps detect SBP. Treat the identified cause alongside HE therapy.

bodies.heading: Do not chase ammonia
bodies.body: Ammonia contributes to pathophysiology but is not a stand-alone diagnostic, severity or dosing test for cirrhosis-associated HE. An elevated value does not prove that confusion is HE, and serial values should not determine lactulose escalation. If a measured value is normal, reconsider competing diagnoses rather than automatically excluding HE. Follow the clinical examination, stool frequency and consistency, hydration, electrolytes and precipitant control. Acute liver failure and urea-cycle disorders require their own specialist pathways; the role of ammonia there should not be extrapolated to routine cirrhosis management.

bodies.heading: Use lactulose to response
bodies.body: Lactulose is a poorly absorbed disaccharide whose colonic metabolism acidifies the lumen, favors trapping ammonia as ammonium and promotes its elimination in stool. It is first-line for overt HE and recurrence prevention after an initial episode. For the verified 10 g/15 mL solution, 20 g equals 30 mL and 30 g equals 45 mL. The book and solution label describe 30 to 45 mL three or four times daily, adjusted to response; initial hourly doses may be used for rapid laxation under monitored acute care. ACG 2026 instead describes 10 to 20 g (15 to 30 mL) every 2 hours until two soft stools for acute grade 2 HE. Use the selected clinical protocol and titrate rather than combining the schedules. Reduce that acute schedule after laxation and titrate maintenance to about 2 to 3 soft stools daily, without continuing hourly dosing automatically.

bodies.heading: Select a safe administration route
bodies.body: Route depends on consciousness, airway protection and gastrointestinal access. Severe aspiration risk requires airway management and a supervised enteral or rectal plan. The verified solution label describes an adult retention enema of 300 mL lactulose solution mixed with 700 mL water or normal saline, retained for 30 to 60 minutes and repeated every 4 to 6 hours when indicated. This is a 1,000 mL mixture; a soap or alkaline cleansing enema is not interchangeable. Resume the prescribed oral regimen when safe, with transition overlap according to the label and clinical plan. Do not treat an enteral tube alone as protection against aspiration.

bodies.heading: Recognize excess catharsis and product restrictions
bodies.body: More diarrhea is not better HE control. Excess lactulose can cause dehydration, hypokalemia and hypernatremia, which can themselves precipitate worsening encephalopathy. Reassess dosing and obtain care for profuse diarrhea, weakness, rising sodium, low potassium or inability to maintain intake. Distinguish usual gas or bloating from severe complications. The verified solution contains galactose and is contraindicated when a low-galactose diet is required; confirm the actual product rather than assuming every formulation has identical excipients. Monitor cognition, bowel quality, fluid status and electrolytes.

bodies.heading: Add rifaximin for recurrence
bodies.body: The US Xifaxan label indicates rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily to reduce overt HE recurrence in adults, with or without food. Lactulose remains first-line outpatient prevention after an initial episode. The 2026 ACG guideline recommends adding rifaximin for recurrent episodes despite lactulose maintenance and also suggests outpatient rifaximin for recurrence prevention. Assess adherence, adequate stool response, medication access and recurrent triggers. Rifaximin does not eliminate the need for lactulose titration, trigger correction or liver follow-up, and the HE schedule differs from the 550 mg three-times-daily 14-day IBS-D regimen.

bodies.heading: Separate acute guidance from the labeled indication
bodies.body: The 2026 ACG guideline conditionally suggests adding rifaximin to lactulose for acute overt HE, with low-certainty evidence. This is a guidance-supported use distinct from the US labeled recurrence-prevention indication; it does not replace stabilization or treatment of precipitants. The book lists a historical acute rifaximin regimen, so do not present that regimen as the only current pathway. High-volume PEG preparations are another conditional inpatient alternative in selected patients, not an instruction to substitute a routine constipation dose at home. The book also lists neomycin and metronidazole; their hearing/kidney toxicity and prolonged-treatment neuropathy concerns make them poor automatic substitutes for the current lactulose/rifaximin pathway.

bodies.heading: Review rifaximin safety and interactions
bodies.body: Rifaximin is contraindicated with hypersensitivity to rifaximin, rifamycin antibiotics or product components. Severe Child-Pugh C impairment increases exposure and requires caution; it is not the same as a blanket labeled contraindication. P-glycoprotein inhibitors such as cyclosporine can further raise exposure. Monitor INR and prothrombin time with warfarin, adjusting warfarin when required. Consider C. difficile when diarrhea is new, persistent or worsening rather than assigning every stool change to lactulose. Stop rifaximin and obtain urgent evaluation for a severe skin reaction or hypersensitivity; the current label includes postmarketing SJS/TEN in cirrhosis.

bodies.heading: Protect nutrition and muscle
bodies.body: Do not routinely restrict protein to treat HE. Muscle loss impairs ammonia handling and worsens frailty. Current ACG guidance targets 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day protein in outpatients with HE, with an individualized nutrition plan, adequate intake and a late-night snack. Vegetable and dairy sources may help tolerance; they should not become a reason to underfeed. BCAA supplementation can help when food alone cannot meet protein needs. Zinc is an adjunct to consider for documented low zinc with persistent symptoms despite lactulose and rifaximin, not a replacement for standard therapy or a universal unqualified dose.

bodies.heading: Reassess nonresponse and shunts
bodies.body: Do not wait for a fixed interval if the patient deteriorates. If cognition has not recovered after 48 to 72 hours of adequate therapy and precipitant treatment, reassess missed infection, drugs, electrolyte or renal abnormalities and alternative neurological disease. Persistent or recurrent HE can reflect spontaneous portosystemic shunts or a prior TIPS; specialists may evaluate imaging and selected shunt interventions. For elective TIPS in decompensated cirrhosis, ACG 2026 recommends rifaximin beginning 14 days beforehand and continuing at least 6 months, with or without previous overt HE. This prophylactic guidance has a different population and timing from emergency treatment.

bodies.heading: Make the discharge plan usable
bodies.body: Give patients and caregivers a written plan for lactulose adjustment, soft-stool goals, medication supply, trigger prevention and whom to contact for worsening confusion, bleeding, fever, profuse diarrhea or inability to take medication. Reconcile sedating and unnecessary medicines and arrange liver and nutrition follow-up. Recent overt HE warrants advice to avoid driving; functional safety requires clinical reassessment rather than clearance by an ammonia result. Recurrent or severe HE should prompt timely transplant evaluation, even when the MELD score appears modest. Support caregivers and reassess long-term therapy with the treating team if the liver disease clinically recompensates.

check.question: A patient taking lactulose has eight watery stools, rising sodium and weakness. Which response is best?
choices: Reassess excess catharsis, reduce the regimen as indicated and address hydration, electrolytes and cognition.
Continue hourly lactulose indefinitely because more stools always improve HE.
Escalate lactulose solely to normalize the latest ammonia value.
Ignore the diarrhea because rifaximin prevents all dehydration-related recurrence.
check.rationale: Excess catharsis can cause fluid loss, hypernatremia and hypokalemia and precipitate HE. Reassess the patient and dosing promptly; the goal is soft stools with safe hydration and clinical recovery. An ammonia result or concurrent rifaximin does not justify uncorrected diarrhea.

cirrhosis-decompensated-085.question: A patient with cirrhosis develops confusion. Which approach best establishes whether overt HE is responsible?
choices: Assess cognition and competing causes while searching for precipitants.
Diagnose HE solely from an elevated ammonia value.
Exclude HE solely because a measured ammonia value is normal.
Diagnose overt HE from isolated asterixis without altered behavior or alertness.
cirrhosis-decompensated-085.rationale: HE is a clinical diagnosis in the appropriate setting after evaluating competing causes. Elevated ammonia is not diagnostic; a normal value prompts reconsideration rather than automatic exclusion. Isolated asterixis is insufficient to establish overt HE.

cirrhosis-decompensated-086.question: A patient with recurrent HE presents with fever, abdominal discomfort and ascites. Which plan is best?
choices: Evaluate infection, including diagnostic paracentesis, and treat HE and the identified trigger.
Treat constipation alone and defer infection assessment until ammonia normalizes.
Assume all confusion is caused by lactulose nonadherence without reviewing the history.
Stop investigation once the ammonia concentration is found to be elevated.
cirrhosis-decompensated-086.rationale: Infection, including SBP, can precipitate HE and can independently alter mental status. Hospitalized ascites with suspected infection warrants diagnostic paracentesis and appropriate infection care. HE treatment proceeds alongside trigger evaluation; ammonia does not exclude other causes.

cirrhosis-decompensated-087.question: A confused patient with cirrhosis has a new unilateral arm weakness. Which plan is safest?
choices: Obtain urgent neurological assessment and indicated brain imaging while evaluating HE.
Attribute the focal deficit to HE and omit neurological evaluation.
Wait for serial ammonia values before assessing possible stroke or bleeding.
Treat with lactulose alone until the focal deficit resolves.
cirrhosis-decompensated-087.rationale: New focal findings suggest a neurological emergency or coexisting disease and require urgent evaluation. Guidance against routine imaging in typical HE without focal findings does not apply here. HE and another disorder can coexist.

cirrhosis-decompensated-088.question: After 60 hours of adequate HE therapy and initial trigger treatment, a patient remains markedly confused. Which approach is best?
choices: Reassess alternative causes, missed precipitants and possible portosystemic shunts.
Escalate catharsis indefinitely despite adequate soft stools and falling intake.
Use persistent ammonia elevation as the only explanation for nonresponse.
Assume a TIPS history eliminates the need to look for infection.
cirrhosis-decompensated-088.rationale: The ACG guideline calls for reassessment after 48 to 72 hours of adequate treatment without mental recovery. Missed infection, medications, metabolic problems, neurological disease or shunts may explain persistent symptoms. Deterioration requires immediate assessment rather than waiting for that interval.

cirrhosis-decompensated-089.question: A prescription calls for 30 g lactulose using a verified 10 g/15 mL oral solution. What volume provides that dose?
choices: 45 mL
15 mL
30 mL
90 mL
cirrhosis-decompensated-089.rationale: Volume = 30 g × 15 mL ÷ 10 g = 45 mL. Confirm the product, route and prescribed frequency. Maintenance dosing is adjusted to about 2 to 3 soft stools daily and clinical response; this calculation does not authorize continuing an acute hourly schedule.

cirrhosis-decompensated-090.question: A caregiver asks how to adjust maintenance lactulose after recovery from overt HE. Which instruction is best?
choices: Follow the prescribed plan for about 2 to 3 soft stools daily and report profuse diarrhea, weakness or recurrent confusion.
Increase the dose until every bowel movement is watery.
Use the ammonia concentration alone to decide each dose.
Stop prevention immediately after the first day of normal cognition.
cirrhosis-decompensated-090.rationale: Stool consistency and frequency, cognition, hydration and electrolytes guide the plan. Excess diarrhea can precipitate dehydration and HE. Recurrence prevention is not automatically stopped after early recovery, and ammonia does not provide a maintenance titration target.

cirrhosis-decompensated-091.question: An obtunded patient with severe HE cannot swallow safely. Which administration plan is appropriate?
choices: Assess airway protection and use a supervised enteral or labeled rectal lactulose plan as appropriate.
Force the oral solution despite aspiration risk.
Assume a nasogastric tube alone prevents aspiration.
Replace lactulose with a soap cleansing enema because all enemas are equivalent.
cirrhosis-decompensated-091.rationale: Route selection must account for airway and aspiration risk. Supervised enteral administration or a labeled lactulose retention enema can be selected after assessment; neither an unprotected oral dose nor a tube alone guarantees safety. Soap or alkaline cleansing enemas are not interchangeable.

cirrhosis-decompensated-092.question: A patient on lactulose has profuse diarrhea, hypernatremia and hypokalemia. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: Excess catharsis can worsen dehydration and precipitate recurrent HE.
These findings prove that the lactulose dose should always be increased.
Watery stool guarantees adequate hydration and excludes HE recurrence.
A normal ammonia value makes electrolyte correction unnecessary.
cirrhosis-decompensated-092.rationale: The book and lactulose label describe fluid loss, hypernatremia and hypokalemia with excessive dosing. Reassess dosing and correct the clinical problem. Stool output or ammonia cannot establish safe hydration or remove the need for electrolyte care.

cirrhosis-decompensated-093.question: An adult has recurrent overt HE despite an appropriate lactulose maintenance plan. Which rifaximin schedule matches the US labeled HE indication?
choices: 550 mg orally twice daily for recurrence-risk reduction.
550 mg orally three times daily for a fixed 14-day HE course.
200 mg orally three times daily for a fixed 3-day HE course.
400 mg intravenously every 8 hours for labeled adult HE prevention.
cirrhosis-decompensated-093.rationale: The US HE recurrence-prevention dose is 550 mg orally twice daily. The 550 mg three-times-daily 14-day schedule is for IBS-D and the 200 mg three-times-daily 3-day schedule is for travelers’ diarrhea. Rifaximin is an oral tablet, not the proposed IV regimen.

cirrhosis-decompensated-094.question: A clinician proposes adding rifaximin to lactulose during acute overt HE. How should the evidence be described?
choices: ACG 2026 conditionally suggests the combination; acute treatment is distinct from the US labeled recurrence-prevention indication.
The US label approves rifaximin as the sole emergency replacement for stabilization.
ACG 2026 prohibits rifaximin during every acute HE episode.
The combination removes the need to assess infection or bleeding.
cirrhosis-decompensated-094.rationale: ACG 2026 conditionally suggests adding rifaximin for acute overt HE with low-certainty evidence. The US label addresses adult recurrence-risk reduction. The combination does not replace airway assessment, lactulose titration or treatment of precipitants.

cirrhosis-decompensated-095.question: A patient with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis takes rifaximin and cyclosporine. Which assessment is best?
choices: Recognize increased rifaximin exposure and review the combined risk with the treating team.
Assume low usual absorption rules out any clinically relevant interaction.
Describe Child-Pugh C as an absolute rifaximin label contraindication.
Switch automatically to long-term neomycin without reviewing hearing or kidney risk.
cirrhosis-decompensated-095.rationale: Severe hepatic impairment increases rifaximin exposure and requires caution; P-glycoprotein inhibition by cyclosporine can further increase exposure. The label does not make Child-Pugh C an absolute contraindication. An automatic long-term neomycin substitution introduces its own substantial toxicity concerns.

cirrhosis-decompensated-096.question: An adult takes rifaximin with warfarin for separate indications. Which monitoring plan is appropriate?
choices: Monitor INR and prothrombin time and adjust warfarin if required.
Stop INR monitoring because rifaximin is usually minimally absorbed.
Double warfarin automatically whenever rifaximin is prescribed.
Replace INR monitoring with serial ammonia concentrations.
cirrhosis-decompensated-096.rationale: The rifaximin label reports INR changes with warfarin and recommends INR/prothrombin-time monitoring and warfarin adjustment when needed. There is no universal automatic dose change. Ammonia does not measure anticoagulation intensity.

wholeObject.question: A confused patient with cirrhosis has a new unilateral arm weakness. Which plan is safest?
choices: Obtain urgent neurological assessment and indicated brain imaging while evaluating HE.
Attribute the focal deficit to HE and omit neurological evaluation.
Wait for serial ammonia values before assessing possible stroke or bleeding.
Treat with lactulose alone until the focal deficit resolves.
wholeObject.rationale: New focal findings suggest a neurological emergency or coexisting disease and require urgent evaluation. Guidance against routine imaging in typical HE without focal findings does not apply here. HE and another disorder can coexist.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: New focal findings suggest a neurological emergency or coexisting disease and require urgent evaluation. Guidance against routine imaging in typical HE without focal findings does not apply here. HE and another disorder can coexist.

wholeObject.question: After 60 hours of adequate HE therapy and initial trigger treatment, a patient remains markedly confused. Which approach is best?
choices: Reassess alternative causes, missed precipitants and possible portosystemic shunts.
Escalate catharsis indefinitely despite adequate soft stools and falling intake.
Use persistent ammonia elevation as the only explanation for nonresponse.
Assume a TIPS history eliminates the need to look for infection.
wholeObject.rationale: The ACG guideline calls for reassessment after 48 to 72 hours of adequate treatment without mental recovery. Missed infection, medications, metabolic problems, neurological disease or shunts may explain persistent symptoms. Deterioration requires immediate assessment rather than waiting for that interval.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: The ACG guideline calls for reassessment after 48 to 72 hours of adequate treatment without mental recovery. Missed infection, medications, metabolic problems, neurological disease or shunts may explain persistent symptoms. Deterioration requires immediate assessment rather than waiting for that interval.

wholeObject.question: A prescription calls for 30 g lactulose using a verified 10 g/15 mL oral solution. What volume provides that dose?
choices: 45 mL
15 mL
30 mL
90 mL
wholeObject.rationale: Volume = 30 g × 15 mL ÷ 10 g = 45 mL. Confirm the product, route and prescribed frequency. Maintenance dosing is adjusted to about 2 to 3 soft stools daily and clinical response; this calculation does not authorize continuing an acute hourly schedule.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Volume = 30 g × 15 mL ÷ 10 g = 45 mL. Confirm the product, route and prescribed frequency. Maintenance dosing is adjusted to about 2 to 3 soft stools daily and clinical response; this calculation does not authorize continuing an acute hourly schedule.

wholeObject.question: A caregiver asks how to adjust maintenance lactulose after recovery from overt HE. Which instruction is best?
choices: Follow the prescribed plan for about 2 to 3 soft stools daily and report profuse diarrhea, weakness or recurrent confusion.
Increase the dose until every bowel movement is watery.
Use the ammonia concentration alone to decide each dose.
Stop prevention immediately after the first day of normal cognition.
wholeObject.rationale: Stool consistency and frequency, cognition, hydration and electrolytes guide the plan. Excess diarrhea can precipitate dehydration and HE. Recurrence prevention is not automatically stopped after early recovery, and ammonia does not provide a maintenance titration target.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Stool consistency and frequency, cognition, hydration and electrolytes guide the plan. Excess diarrhea can precipitate dehydration and HE. Recurrence prevention is not automatically stopped after early recovery, and ammonia does not provide a maintenance titration target.

wholeObject.question: An obtunded patient with severe HE cannot swallow safely. Which administration plan is appropriate?
choices: Assess airway protection and use a supervised enteral or labeled rectal lactulose plan as appropriate.
Force the oral solution despite aspiration risk.
Assume a nasogastric tube alone prevents aspiration.
Replace lactulose with a soap cleansing enema because all enemas are equivalent.
wholeObject.rationale: Route selection must account for airway and aspiration risk. Supervised enteral administration or a labeled lactulose retention enema can be selected after assessment; neither an unprotected oral dose nor a tube alone guarantees safety. Soap or alkaline cleansing enemas are not interchangeable.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Route selection must account for airway and aspiration risk. Supervised enteral administration or a labeled lactulose retention enema can be selected after assessment; neither an unprotected oral dose nor a tube alone guarantees safety. Soap or alkaline cleansing enemas are not interchangeable.

wholeObject.question: A patient on lactulose has profuse diarrhea, hypernatremia and hypokalemia. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: Excess catharsis can worsen dehydration and precipitate recurrent HE.
These findings prove that the lactulose dose should always be increased.
Watery stool guarantees adequate hydration and excludes HE recurrence.
A normal ammonia value makes electrolyte correction unnecessary.
wholeObject.rationale: The book and lactulose label describe fluid loss, hypernatremia and hypokalemia with excessive dosing. Reassess dosing and correct the clinical problem. Stool output or ammonia cannot establish safe hydration or remove the need for electrolyte care.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: The book and lactulose label describe fluid loss, hypernatremia and hypokalemia with excessive dosing. Reassess dosing and correct the clinical problem. Stool output or ammonia cannot establish safe hydration or remove the need for electrolyte care.

wholeObject.question: An adult has recurrent overt HE despite an appropriate lactulose maintenance plan. Which rifaximin schedule matches the US labeled HE indication?
choices: 550 mg orally twice daily for recurrence-risk reduction.
550 mg orally three times daily for a fixed 14-day HE course.
200 mg orally three times daily for a fixed 3-day HE course.
400 mg intravenously every 8 hours for labeled adult HE prevention.
wholeObject.rationale: The US HE recurrence-prevention dose is 550 mg orally twice daily. The 550 mg three-times-daily 14-day schedule is for IBS-D and the 200 mg three-times-daily 3-day schedule is for travelers’ diarrhea. Rifaximin is an oral tablet, not the proposed IV regimen.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: The US HE recurrence-prevention dose is 550 mg orally twice daily. The 550 mg three-times-daily 14-day schedule is for IBS-D and the 200 mg three-times-daily 3-day schedule is for travelers’ diarrhea. Rifaximin is an oral tablet, not the proposed IV regimen.

wholeObject.question: A clinician proposes adding rifaximin to lactulose during acute overt HE. How should the evidence be described?
choices: ACG 2026 conditionally suggests the combination; acute treatment is distinct from the US labeled recurrence-prevention indication.
The US label approves rifaximin as the sole emergency replacement for stabilization.
ACG 2026 prohibits rifaximin during every acute HE episode.
The combination removes the need to assess infection or bleeding.
wholeObject.rationale: ACG 2026 conditionally suggests adding rifaximin for acute overt HE with low-certainty evidence. The US label addresses adult recurrence-risk reduction. The combination does not replace airway assessment, lactulose titration or treatment of precipitants.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: ACG 2026 conditionally suggests adding rifaximin for acute overt HE with low-certainty evidence. The US label addresses adult recurrence-risk reduction. The combination does not replace airway assessment, lactulose titration or treatment of precipitants.

wholeObject.question: A patient with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis takes rifaximin and cyclosporine. Which assessment is best?
choices: Recognize increased rifaximin exposure and review the combined risk with the treating team.
Assume low usual absorption rules out any clinically relevant interaction.
Describe Child-Pugh C as an absolute rifaximin label contraindication.
Switch automatically to long-term neomycin without reviewing hearing or kidney risk.
wholeObject.rationale: Severe hepatic impairment increases rifaximin exposure and requires caution; P-glycoprotein inhibition by cyclosporine can further increase exposure. The label does not make Child-Pugh C an absolute contraindication. An automatic long-term neomycin substitution introduces its own substantial toxicity concerns.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Severe hepatic impairment increases rifaximin exposure and requires caution; P-glycoprotein inhibition by cyclosporine can further increase exposure. The label does not make Child-Pugh C an absolute contraindication. An automatic long-term neomycin substitution introduces its own substantial toxicity concerns.

wholeObject.question: An adult takes rifaximin with warfarin for separate indications. Which monitoring plan is appropriate?
choices: Monitor INR and prothrombin time and adjust warfarin if required.
Stop INR monitoring because rifaximin is usually minimally absorbed.
Double warfarin automatically whenever rifaximin is prescribed.
Replace INR monitoring with serial ammonia concentrations.
wholeObject.rationale: The rifaximin label reports INR changes with warfarin and recommends INR/prothrombin-time monitoring and warfarin adjustment when needed. There is no universal automatic dose change. Ammonia does not measure anticoagulation intensity.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: The rifaximin label reports INR changes with warfarin and recommends INR/prothrombin-time monitoring and warfarin adjustment when needed. There is no universal automatic dose change. Ammonia does not measure anticoagulation intensity.

discrepancies.issue: Generic repeated HE prompts have multiple defensible true statements or several harmful answers.
discrepancies.resolution: Replace all 12 with distinct clinical cases, one best answer and explicit rationale; IDs, answer indexes, difficulty and anchors remain stable.

discrepancies.issue: The book includes serial ammonia in drug monitoring and an ammonia-reduction treatment framing.
discrepancies.resolution: Teach the current clinical examination, precipitant and bowel/hydration approach; normal ammonia prompts a broader differential, not automatic exclusion. Separate acute-liver-failure ammonia pathways.

discrepancies.issue: The book limits animal protein and uses a 1 to 1.5 g/kg/day target.
discrepancies.resolution: Use current ACG outpatient 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day, explicitly reject routine protein restriction, and preserve adequate intake with appropriate dietary sources and muscle care.

discrepancies.issue: Book/solution label initial hourly 20 to 30 g dosing differs from ACG 2026 grade-2 acute 10 to 20 g every 2 hours.
discrepancies.resolution: Show source-specific alternatives with monitored clinical-protocol selection; do not combine schedules and reduce after laxation. Independently verify grams/mL.

discrepancies.issue: The book gives a historical 400 mg every-8-hour acute rifaximin course; US HE label addresses recurrence.
discrepancies.resolution: Distinguish 2026 conditional acute add-on guidance, low evidence certainty and labeled 550 mg twice-daily recurrence prevention. Do not present the historical acute course as the only modern pathway.

discrepancies.issue: Book neomycin/metronidazole alternatives and an unqualified zinc salt dose can invite unsafe automatic substitution.
discrepancies.resolution: Retain toxicity boundaries and current standard therapy; discuss zinc only as a deficiency-qualified adjunct, without implying salt mass equals elemental zinc.

discrepancies.issue: Minimal usual rifaximin absorption can hide impaired-liver/P-gp exposure and warfarin/skin safety.
discrepancies.resolution: Include severe impairment caution without false absolute contraindication, P-gp and INR monitoring, CDI and current SJS/TEN language.

discrepancies.issue: Routine oral administration or tubes can be mistaken for protected airway care.
discrepancies.resolution: Require airway/route assessment and verified solution-label rectal preparation, retaining aspiration and transition qualifiers.

discrepancies.issue: Older TIPS recommendations predate current ACG 2026 preventive timing and population.
discrepancies.resolution: Clearly attribute elective decompensated-cirrhosis prophylaxis 14 days before/at least six months after to ACG 2026; no emergency TIPS delay or universal historical pathway claimed.
